routine.label: Routine vaccines
text: Make sure you are up-to-date on all routine vaccines before every trip. Some of these vaccines include
• Chickenpox (Varicella)
• Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis (DTaP, Tdap, or Td)
• Flu (influenza)
• Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR)
• Polio
• Shingles

covid19.label: COVID-19
text: All eligible travelers should be up to date with their COVID-19 vaccines. Please see Your COVID-19 Vaccination for more information.

cholera.label: Cholera
text: Active cholera transmission is widespread in Afghanistan. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Afghanistan.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers younger than 60 years old traveling to Afghanistan. Unvaccinated travelers 60 years and older may get vaccinated before traveling to Afghanistan.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Afghanistan take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All areas <2,500 m (<8,200 ft) elevation (April–December)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. vivax (primarily)
• P. falciparum (less commonly)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
Updated April 23, 2025
See footnotes

areas: All areas <2,500 m (<8,200 ft) elevation (April–December)

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

polio.label: Polio
text: In Afghanistan, poliovirus has been identified in the past year.
Travelers to Afghanistan are at increased risk of exposure to poliovirus.

Vaccine recommendations: Adults traveling to Afghanistan who received a complete polio vaccination series as children may receive a single lifetime booster dose of inactivated polio vaccine; travelers who are unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated should receive a complete polio vaccination series before travel. Children who are not fully vaccinated will be considered for an accelerated vaccination schedule.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Afghanistan.
If rabies exposures occur while in Afghanistan, rabies vaccines are typically not readily available.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Recommended for most travelers.
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements: Vaccine is not required.
Updated April 23, 2025

text: Make sure you are up-to-date on all routine vaccines before every trip. Some of these vaccines include
• Chickenpox (Varicella)
• Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis (DTaP, Tdap, or Td)
• Flu (influenza)
• Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR)
• Polio
• Shingles

covid19.label: COVID-19
text: All eligible travelers should be up to date with their COVID-19 vaccines. Please see Your COVID-19 Vaccination for more information.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Antigua and Barbuda.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Antigua and Barbuda.

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are not commonly found in Antigua and Barbuda.
If rabies exposures occur while in Antigua and Barbuda, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Consider getting a typhoid vaccine if you might:
• Travel to areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water, including rural areas
• Spend a long time in Antigua and Barbuda, such as a month or more
• Visit friends or relatives
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements:
• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥1 year old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Japanese encephalitis is mainly a concern in the Murray River, and the Outer Torres Strait Islands area.
Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or traveling at times outside of the Japanese encephalitis season.

• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Bangladesh take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas

• Districts of Chittagong Hill Tract (Bandarban, Khagrachari, and Rangamati); and the following districts: Chattogram (Chittagong) and Cox’s Bazar (in Chattogram [Chittagong] Division); Mymensingh, Netrakona, and Sherpur (in Mymensingh Division); Kurigram (in Rangpur Division); Habiganj, Moulvibazar, Sunamganj, and Sylhet (in Sylhet Division)
• No malaria transmission in Dhaka (the capital)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. falciparum (80%)
• P. vivax (20%)
• P. malariae (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

text: There is elevated chikungunya risk in Brazil. Chikungunya vaccination may be considered for people traveling or moving to this location if they are planning to stay for an extended period of time (for example, 6 months or more).

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Brazil.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers younger than 60 years old traveling to Brazil. Unvaccinated travelers 60 years and older may get vaccinated before traveling to Brazil.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Brazil take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All areas in the states of Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Rondônia, and Roraima
• Present in the states of Maranhão, Mato Grosso, and Pará, but rare cases in their capital cities (São Luis [capital of Maranhão], Cuiabá [capital of Mato Grosso], Belém [capital of Pará])
• Rare cases and sporadic foci of transmission in rural and forested areas in the states of Espírito Santo, Goiás, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso do Sul, Piauí, Rio de Janeiro, São Paolo, and Tocantins
• No malaria transmission in the cities of Brasília (the capital), Rio de Janeiro, or São Paolo
• No malaria transmission at Iguaçu Falls
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. vivax (90%)
• P. falciparum (10%)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
• Areas with rare cases: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. rabies.label: Rabies

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid

Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are sometimes found in Colombia.
Rabies is also present in bats.
If rabies exposures occur while in Colombia, rabies vaccines are typically available throughout most of the country.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Consider getting a typhoid vaccine if you might:
• Travel to areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water, including rural areas
• Spend a long time in Colombia, such as a month or more
• Visit friends or relatives
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations:
• Vaccine is recommended for all travelers ≥9 months old except as follows
• Vaccine is generally not recommended for travel limited to the cities of Barranquilla, Cali, Cartagena, or Medellín.
• Vaccine is not recommended for travel limited to areas >2,300 m (7,550 ft) elevation, the archipelago department of San Andrés and Providencia, or the city of Bogotá (the capital).
Country entry requirements:
• Vaccine is required for all arriving travelers ≥1 year old.
• Country entry requirements are subject to change. Check with the embassies or consulates on your itinerary to confirm entry requirements before departure.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Comoros take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.

• All

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are not commonly found in the Faroe Islands.
If rabies exposures occur while in the Faroe Islands, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to French Guiana.

Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of French Guiana take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas

• Areas associated with gold mining, primarily the communes near the border with Brazil and Suriname, especially Régina and Saint-Georges-de-l’Oyapock; also, the communes of Kourou, Matoury, and Saint-élie
• No malaria transmission in coastal areas west of Kourou
• No malaria transmission in Cayenne City (the capital)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. vivax (85%)
• P. falciparum (15%)
• P. malariae (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
Updated April 23, 2025

text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

polio.label: Polio
text: In Germany, poliovirus has been identified in the past year.

Children who are not fully vaccinated will be considered for an accelerated vaccination schedule.

For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Ghana take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Transmission areas

Drug resistance

Species

• P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax (less commonly)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

chikungunya.label: Chikungunya
text: All travelers should take steps to prevent mosquito bites. Chikungunya vaccination is generally not recommended. Travelers who wish to consider vaccination can visit “What to consider before traveling” on the chikungunya vaccines page to learn more.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Guatemala.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers younger than 60 years old traveling to Guatemala. Unvaccinated travelers 60 years and older may get vaccinated before traveling to Guatemala.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Guatemala take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• Primarily in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Baja Verapaz, Escuintla, Izabal, and Petén
• Few cases reported in other departments
• No malaria transmission in the cities of Antigua or Guatemala City (the capital)
• No malaria transmission at Lake Atitlán
Drug resistance
• None
Species
• P. vivax (99%)
• P. falciparum (1%)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Departments of Alta Verapaz, Baja Verapaz, Escuintla, Izabal, and Petén: Atovaquone-proguanil, chloroquine, doxycycline, mefloquine, primaquine, tafenoquine
• Other areas with reported malaria transmission: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)
Updated April 23, 2025

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are sometimes found in Guatemala.
Rabies is also present in bats.
If rabies exposures occur while in Guatemala, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

text: Areas of active cholera transmission are localized to the counties of Garissa (last case reported in the past 3 months), Migori (last case reported 6-9 months ago), Mombasa (last case reported 9-12 months ago), Nairobi (last case reported 9-12 months ago), Narok (last case reported 9-12 months ago), and Turkana (last case reported 9-12 months ago)

in Kenya. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Kenya take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All areas (including game parks) <2,500 m (<8,200 ft) elevation; rare cases in the highly urbanized central part of the city of Nairobi (the capital)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. falciparum (primarily)
• P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax (less commonly)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
• Highly urbanized central part of the city of Nairobi: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)

• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets

Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Laos take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• Present in the southern part of the country in the provinces of Attapeu, Champasak, Khammouane, Salavan, Savannakhet, and Sekong
• Rare cases in the northern part of the country
• None in the cities of Luang Prabang and Vientiane (the capital)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine and mefloquine
Species
• P. vivax (55%)
• P. falciparum (45%)
• P. knowlesi, P. malariae, and P. ovale (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• In the provinces of Attapeu, Champasak, Khammouane, Salavan, Savannakhet, and Sekong: Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, tafenoquine
• Northern part of the country: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)

It is recommended for travelers who will be doing higher risk activities, such as visiting smaller cities, villages, or rural areas where a traveler might get infected through food or water. It is recommended for travelers who plan on eating street food.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to the Madeira Islands.

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are not commonly found in the Madeira Islands.
If rabies exposures occur while in the Madeira Islands, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

chikungunya.label: Chikungunya

cholera.label: Cholera
text: Active cholera transmission is widespread in Malawi. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Malawi.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers younger than 60 years old traveling to Malawi. Unvaccinated travelers 60 years and older may get vaccinated before traveling to Malawi.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Malawi take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. falciparum (primarily)
• P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax (less commonly)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Malaysia take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Transmission areas
• Zoonotic transmission of P. knowlesi malaria occurs in rural, forested areas
• No malaria transmission in other areas, including Kuala Lumpur (the capital), in Penang State, on Penang Island, or in George Town (capital of Penang State)
Drug resistance
• Previously, chloroquine
Species
• P. knowlesi (primarily)
• Previously, P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• In rural, forested areas: atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

polio.label: Polio
text: In Pakistan, poliovirus has been identified in the past year.
Travelers to Pakistan are at increased risk of exposure to poliovirus.

Vaccine recommendations: Adults traveling to Pakistan who received a complete polio vaccination series as children may receive a single lifetime booster dose of inactivated polio vaccine; travelers who are unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated should receive a complete polio vaccination series before travel. Children who are not fully vaccinated will be considered for an accelerated vaccination schedule.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Pakistan.
If rabies exposures occur while in Pakistan, rabies vaccines are typically not readily available.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Recommended for most travelers.
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.
A significant proportion of Salmonella Typhi strains found in Pakistan are extensively drug resistant but remain susceptible to azithromycin and carbapenems (more information).

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever

• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥1 year old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Panama take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• The provinces of Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí, Colón, Darién, Panamá, Panamá Oeste, and Veraguas
• The indigenous provinces (comarcas indígena) of Emberá, Kuna Yala (also spelled Guna Yala) and Ngäbe-Buglé
• Rare cases in other parts of the country
• No malaria transmission in the Canal Zone or in Panama City (the capital)
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine (east of the Panama Canal)
Species
• P. vivax (97%)
• P. falciparum (3%)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Darién, Emberá, Kuna Yala, and Panamá Provinces : Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, primaquine, tafenoquine
• Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí, Colón, Ngäbe-Buglé, Panamá Oeste, and Veraguas Provinces: Atovaquone-proguanil, chloroquine, doxycycline, mefloquine, primaquine, tafenoquine
• All other areas with malaria transmission: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

cholera.label: Cholera
text: Cholera is presumed to be present in the Philippines. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to the Philippines.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to the Philippines.

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of the Philippines take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• Province of Palawan and the Mindanao Island group
• No malaria transmission in metropolitan Manila (the capital) or other urban areas
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. falciparum (85%)
• P. vivax (15%)
• P. knowlesi, P. malariae, and P. ovale (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
Updated April 23, 2025

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in the Philippines.
If rabies exposures occur while in the Philippines, rabies vaccines are typically available throughout most of the country.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Recommended for most travelers.
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Saint Martin.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Saint Martin.

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are not commonly found in Saint Martin.
If rabies exposures occur while in Saint Martin, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Consider getting a typhoid vaccine if you might:
• Travel to areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water, including rural areas
• Spend a long time in Saint Martin, such as a month or more
• Visit friends or relatives
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements:
• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥1 year old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.

TBE vaccine is recommended for persons who will have extensive exposure to ticks based on their planned outdoor activities and itinerary.
TBE vaccine may be considered for persons who might engage in outdoor activities in areas ticks are likely to be found.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements: Vaccine is not required.
Updated April 23, 2025

routine.label: Routine vaccines
text: Make sure you are up-to-date on all routine vaccines before every trip. Some of these vaccines include
• Chickenpox (Varicella)
• Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis (DTaP, Tdap, or Td)
• Flu (influenza)
• Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR)
• Polio
• Shingles

covid19.label: COVID-19
text: All eligible travelers should be up to date with their COVID-19 vaccines. Please see Your COVID-19 Vaccination for more information.

chikungunya.label: Chikungunya
text: All travelers should take steps to prevent mosquito bites. Chikungunya vaccination is generally not recommended. Travelers who wish to consider vaccination can visit “What to consider before traveling” on the chikungunya vaccines page to learn more.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Seychelles.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Seychelles.

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are not commonly found in Seychelles.
If rabies exposures occur while in Seychelles, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Recommended for most travelers.
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements:
• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥1 year old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.

chikungunya.label: Chikungunya
text: All travelers should take steps to prevent mosquito bites. Chikungunya vaccination is generally not recommended. Travelers who wish to consider vaccination can visit “What to consider before traveling” on the chikungunya vaccines page to learn more.

cholera.label: Cholera
text: Active cholera transmission is widespread in Somalia. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Somalia.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Somalia.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Somalia take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine

• P. falciparum (90%)
• P. vivax (5–10%)
• P. malariae and P. ovale (rare)

• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade

polio.label: Polio

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis

• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Uzbekistan.
If rabies exposures occur while in Uzbekistan, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Consider getting a typhoid vaccine if you might:
• Travel to areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water, including rural areas
• Spend a long time in Uzbekistan, such as a month or more
• Visit friends or relatives
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Vanuatu.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Vanuatu.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Vanuatu take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. vivax (primarily)
• P. falciparum and P. ovale (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine

je.label: Japanese Encephalitis
text: Recommended for travelers who
• Are moving to an area with Japanese encephalitis to live
• Spend long periods of time, such as a month or more, in areas with Japanese encephalitis
• Frequently travel to areas with Japanese encephalitis
Consider vaccination for travelers

• Spending less than a month in areas with Japanese encephalitis but will be doing activities that increase risk of infection, such as visiting rural areas, hiking or camping, or staying in places without air conditioning, screens, or bed nets
• Going to areas with Japanese encephalitis who are uncertain of their activities or how long they will be there
Not recommended for travelers planning short-term travel to urban areas or travel to areas with no clear Japanese encephalitis season.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to certain areas of Vietnam take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• Rural areas only; rare cases in the Mekong and Red River Deltas
• None in the cities of Da Nang, Hai Phong, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon), Nha Trang, and Quy Nhon
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine and mefloquine
Species
• P. vivax (55%)
• P. falciparum (44%)
• P. knowlesi, P. malariae, and P. ovale (rare)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Provinces of Bình Dương, Bình Phước, Đắk Lắk, Đắk Nông, Gia Lai, Khánh Hòa, Kon Tum, Lâm Đồng, Ninh Thuận, Tây Ninh: Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, tafenoquine
• All other areas with malaria transmission (except Mekong and Red River Deltas): Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
• Mekong and Red River Deltas: No chemoprophylaxis recommended (insect bite precautions and mosquito avoidance only)
Updated April 23, 2025

text: In Zambia, poliovirus has been identified in the past year.
Travelers to Zambia are at increased risk of exposure to poliovirus.

Vaccine recommendations: Adults traveling to Zambia who received a complete polio vaccination series as children may receive a single lifetime booster dose of inactivated polio vaccine; travelers who are unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated should receive a complete polio vaccination series before travel. Children who are not fully vaccinated will be considered for an accelerated vaccination schedule.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Zambia.
Rabies is also present in some terrestrial wildlife species.
If rabies exposures occur while in Zambia, rabies vaccines may only be available in larger suburban/urban medical facilities.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Recommended for most travelers.
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations:
• Vaccine is generally not recommended for travel to North-Western Province or Western Province.
• Vaccine is not recommended for travel to any areas not listed above.
Country entry requirements:
• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥1 year old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.
Updated April 23, 2025

routine.label: Routine vaccines
text: Make sure you are up-to-date on all routine vaccines before every trip. Some of these vaccines include
• Chickenpox (Varicella)
• Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis (DTaP, Tdap, or Td)
• Flu (influenza)
• Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR)
• Polio
• Shingles

covid19.label: COVID-19
text: All eligible travelers should be up to date with their COVID-19 vaccines. Please see Your COVID-19 Vaccination for more information.

cholera.label: Cholera
text: Areas of active cholera transmission are localized to Manicaland (last case reported in the past 3 months), Mashonaland Central (last case reported 6-9 months ago), Mashonaland East (last case reported 9-12 months ago), and Midlands (last case reported in the past 3 months)

in Zimbabwe. Cholera is rare in travelers. Certain factors may increase the risk of getting cholera or having severe disease (more information). Avoiding unsafe food and water and washing your hands can also help prevent cholera.
Vaccination may be considered for children and adults who are traveling to areas of active cholera transmission.

hepA.label: Hepatitis A
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers one year old or older going to Zimbabwe.
Infants 6 to 11 months old should also be vaccinated against Hepatitis A. The dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.
Travelers allergic to a vaccine component should receive a single dose of immune globulin, which provides effective protection for up to 2 months depending on dosage given.

Unvaccinated travelers who are over 40 years old, are immunocompromised, or have chronic medical conditions planning to depart to a risk area in less than 2 weeks should get the initial dose of vaccine and at the same appointment receive immune globulin.

hepB.label: Hepatitis B
text: Recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages traveling to Zimbabwe.

malaria.label: Malaria
text: CDC recommends that travelers going to Zimbabwe take prescription medicine to prevent malaria. Depending on the medicine you take, you will need to start taking this medicine multiple days before your trip, as well as during and after your trip. Talk to your doctor about which malaria medication you should take.
Transmission areas
• All
Drug resistance
• Chloroquine
Species
• P. falciparum (primarily)
• P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax (less commonly)
Recommended chemoprophylaxis
• Atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, tafenoquine
Updated April 23, 2025

measles.label: Measles
text: Cases of measles are on the rise worldwide. Travelers are at risk of measles if they have not been fully vaccinated at least two weeks prior to departure, or have not had measles in the past, and travel internationally to areas where measles is spreading.

All international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, including an early dose for infants 6–11 months, according to CDC’s measles vaccination recommendations for international travel.

mpox.label: Monkeypox
text: Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for any adult who anticipates any of the following activities during travel:
• Sexual or intimate contact with a new partner
• Sexual or intimate contact at a commercial sex venue, like a sex club or bathhouse
• Sexual or intimate contact in exchange for money, goods, drugs, or other trade
• Sexual or intimate contact in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party, or festival

Get your first monkeypox vaccine at least 6 weeks before traveling if you can, or as far as possible before travel if fewer than 6 weeks before you leave. Two doses of vaccine, given 4 weeks apart, are recommended. After completing your first and second vaccine doses it takes about 2 more weeks to get the best protection against monkeypox. Whether or not you've been vaccinated, continue to take steps to reduce your risk of getting monkeypox while you are away.

rabies.label: Rabies
text: Dogs infected with rabies are commonly found in Zimbabwe.
Rabies is also present in some terrestrial wildlife species.
If rabies exposures occur while in Zimbabwe, rabies vaccines are typically available throughout most of the country.

Rabies pre-exposure vaccination considerations include whether travelers 1) will be performing occupational or recreational activities that increase risk for exposure to potentially rabid animals and 2) might have difficulty getting prompt access to safe post-exposure prophylaxis.
Please consult with a healthcare provider to determine whether you should receive pre-exposure vaccination before travel.
For more information, see country rabies status assessments.

typhoid.label: Typhoid
text: Consider getting a typhoid vaccine if you might:
• Travel to areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water, including rural areas
• Spend a long time in Zimbabwe, such as a month or more
• Visit friends or relatives
Typhoid vaccine is not 100% effective. Practicing safe food and water habits, including washing hands at key times, can also help prevent typhoid fever.

yellowFever.label: Yellow Fever
text: CDC recommendations: Vaccine is not recommended.
Country entry requirements:
• Direct travel from United States: Vaccine is not required.

• Travel from countries with risk for YF virus transmission: Vaccine is required for travelers ≥9 months old; this includes >12-hour airport transits or layovers in countries with risk for YF virus transmission.
